obtained.how: MDIFW's own PDF of the plan, from the agency's www1.maine.gov server (same path as the cited URL; www.maine.gov refuses scripts with 403); 33 pages with a text layer; Tables 1 and 2 read on the page images (the layout text scrambles both)

bibliography.note: Title page: 'NON-SPORT AND COMMERICIAL MANAGEMENT PLAN' (sic), Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Division of Fisheries and Hatcheries, prepared by Nels Kramer, Assistant Regional Fisheries Biologist, Region F, January 2002. The ledger entry is right; the author's first name (Nels) and 'Region F' may be added.

claims.claim: MDIFW's non-sport plan lists sea-run alewife in 102 Maine lakes, blacknose dace in 436, American eel in 683, fallfish in 461 and banded killifish in 363
claims.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3), Table 1 'List of all Non-Sport Fish in Maine' (read on the page image)
claims.conditions: number of Maine lakes and ponds in which the species has been recorded (with total acreage); the text warns that past surveys were imprecise and often recorded only 'minnows', so a more intensive survey 'would no doubt increase these numbers'
claims.note: The layout text shifts Table 1's numbers against the species (it puts 462 beside golden shiner and 851 beside white sucker); on the page image golden shiner is 851 lakes and common shiner 462.

claims.claim: the plan lists white sucker in 1,206 Maine lakes and yellow perch in 818
claims.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3), Table 1; yellow perch also p. 5 text; white sucker also p. 11, Table 4 (state total)
claims.conditions: lakes and ponds; white sucker 1,206 lakes and 893,572 acres (Tables 1 and 4); p. 5: yellow perch 'is found in 818 lakes and ponds in Maine'

claims.claim: Maine yellow perch 'seldom exceed 12 inches … probably average closer to 8 inches'
claims.quote: In Maine yellow perch seldom exceed 12 inches in length, and adults probably average
claims.conditions: '… closer to 8 inches in most waters'; adults; length type not stated
claims.note: p. 12 adds the agency's explanation: low fertility, short growing seasons and interspecific competition, so 'yellow perch in Maine are commonly small in size'.

claims.claim: Maine yellow perch spawn 'in early spring when water temperatures are in the mid 40s' °F (≈ 7 °C)
claims.quote: Yellow perch spawn in early spring when water temperatures are in the mid 40's
claims.conditions: no unit is printed; °F follows from the context (mid-40s °F = about 6.7–7.8 °C); eggs in a gelatinous ribbon over vegetation or submerged branches of fallen trees

claims.conditions: statewide generalization, no data; Table 2 gives size at maturity 8 to 14 inches
claims.note: Rewrite as: suckers 'up to 4 or 5 pounds are common in some lake environments' (1.8–2.3 kg) (Kramer 2002).

tried.note: maine.gov refuses scripts; the www1.maine.gov URL served the PDF

notes: Corrections are wording and conditions, not numbers: the white sucker weight is 'up to 4 or 5 pounds … common in some lake environments', the fallfish '5 to 8 inches' is Kramer's size at maturity, and the banded killifish size at maturity is 2–3 in in Table 2 but 2–4 in in the text. Other useful material: (1) Table 2 marks banded killifish 'Indigenous: No' (and golden shiner 'No'), one of the sources behind §2.5's 'sources disagree on whether banded killifish is native'. (2) p. 4: the fallfish 'builds the most commonly observed nest of the minnows found in Maine. The males construct a communal nest of stones up to 2 inches in diameter, as large as 6 feet across and 2 feet high' — a citable source for Table 3.5-2's 'communal mounds up to ≈ 1.8 m across (secondary accounts)'; but Trial et al. 1983a say 'Each nest is constructed by a single male' (communal spawning on it). (3) Table 1: golden shiner in 851 Maine lakes (the layout text misplaces it as 462). (4) p. 12: Maine yellow perch 'are commonly small in size' because of 'the relatively low fertility of Maine waters, short growing seasons, and inter-specific competition'; Maine sets no size or bag limit for yellow perch. (5) Table 2's blacknose dace row: age at maturity 2 years, maximum age 3 to 4 years, size at maturity 2 to 2½ inches.
